nodes.name: Hydrothermal Synthesis of Ni-BDC
nodes.procedure: Ni-BDC nanosheet arrays were synthesized via a modified hydrothermal method and uniformly deposited on carbon fibers (detailed experimental procedure in Supporting Information).
nodes.source_text: Initially, Ni-BDC is synthesized via a modified hydrothermal method (see the Supporting Information for the experimental details). Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) images show that Ni-BDC ultrathin nanosheet arrays were uniformly deposited on carbon fibers (Figure S1).

unit_operations.name: Hydrothermal Reaction
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: Ni-BDC is synthesized via a modified hydrothermal method

nodes.name: Ion Exchange Ni-BDC to NiRu-BDC
nodes.procedure: Ni-BDC underwent cation-exchange treatment with Ru precursor to obtain NiRu-BDC, retaining the original nanosheet array morphology. EDS and XPS confirmed successful Ruδ+ exchange into Ni-BDC (Figures S3 and S4). XRD, FT-IR, and Raman confirmed no change in structure.
nodes.source_text: After a cation-exchange treatment, the NiRu-BDC was obtained, retaining the original nanosheet array shape (Figure S2). Energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) prove that Ruδ+ is successfully exchanged into Ni-BDC (Figures S3 and S4).

nodes.name: Pyrolysis of NiRu-BDC to NiRu/C
nodes.procedure: NiRu-BDC was pyrolyzed at 800°C (guided by TGA, Figure S8) to ensure complete decomposition and high crystallinity, yielding NiRu/C with well-preserved nanosheet arrays containing ultrafine 8-10 nm nanoparticles confined in ultrathin porous carbon nanosheets.
nodes.source_text: Guided by the thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) result (Figure S8), 800°C was chosen for pyrolyzing Ni-BDC and NiRu-BDC to ensure thorough decomposition and achieve high crystallinity. FESEM images show the well-preserved nanosheet arrays of NiRu/C with ultrafine nanoparticles (8-10 nm)...

unit_operations.name: High-temperature Pyrolysis
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: 800°C was chosen for pyrolyzing NiRu-BDC to ensure thorough decomposition and achieve high crystallinity

nodes.description: HER performance in 1.0 M KOH (three-electrode setup)
nodes.source_text: The HER performance in 1.0 M KOH reveals NiRu/C s superior catalytic activity... ultralow overpotentials of 48, 99, and 133 mV at current densities of 10, 50, and 100 mA cm^{-2}... mass activity enhancement over commercial Pt/C, achieving 3.60 and 18.68 A mg_{Ru}^{-1} at overpotentials of 100 and 200 mV... Tafel slope of NiRu/C is 34 mV dec^{-1}... Tafel plots from operando electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)... lowest Tafel slope (28 mV dec^{-1})... double-layer capacitance (C_{dl}) of NiRu/C reaches 55 mF cm^{-2}... After 30000 cyclic voltammetry (CV) cycles... chronoamperometry tests with a potential of -220 mV vs. RHE and could stably run over 50 h

NiRu/C demonstrates superior OER activity with a 284 mV overpotential at 10 mA cm^{-2}... mass activities of 0.87 and 1.85 A mg_{Ru}^{-1} at 200 and 300 mV overpotentials... lower Tafel slope (57 mV dec^{-1})... higher C_{dl} of NiRu/C (11 mF cm^{-2})... After 30000 CV cycles... maintaining the activity with minimal decline after continuous operation for over 150 h... higher redox peak intensity of NiRu/C with a Faraday charge of 330 mC

NiRu/C||NiRu/C requires a low cell voltage of 1.47 V to deliver a current density of 10 mA cm^{-2}... excellent durability with a 90% activity retention after continuous operation of 160 h... Faradaic efficiency (FE) is determined to be approximately 100%

NiRu/C catalysts display superior bifunctional performance, achieving an industrial current density of 1 A cm^{-2} at 1.75 V... operated for more than 350 h at 1 A cm^{-2} with a negligible increase in voltage
Tafel plots from operando electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)... Ni/C (110 mV dec^{-1})... double-layer capacitance (C_{dl}) of NiRu/C reaches 55 mF cm^{-2}, much higher than Ni/C
outperforming Ni/C (350 mV)... lower Tafel slope (57 mV dec^{-1}) than Ni/C (87 mV dec^{-1})... higher C_{dl} of NiRu/C (11 mF cm^{-2}) compared to Ni/C (3 mF cm^{-2})

nodes.characterization_summary: NiRu/C shows well-preserved nanosheet arrays with ultrafine nanoparticles (8-10 nm) confined in ultrathin porous carbon nanosheets.
nodes.evidence_snippet: FESEM images show the well-preserved nanosheet arrays of NiRu/C with ultrafine nanoparticles (8 - 10 nm) confined in ultrathin porous carbon nanosheets (Figure 1b-d).

nodes.characterization_summary: NiRu/C shows lattice spacing of 0.20 and 0.18 nm corresponding to (111) and (200) crystal planes of fcc Ni; evenly dispersed bright spots indicate isolated Ru atoms anchored on Ni nanoparticles without aggregation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC HAADF-STEM) images show that the lattice spacing of 0.20 and 0.18 nm in both NiRu/C (Figure 1e,f) ... some evenly dispersed bright spots can be observed in NiRu nanoparticles without obvious aggregation (Figures 1f,g, and S11).

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS elemental mapping verifies Ru atoms selectively anchor on Ni surfaces rather than carbon substrates in NiRu/C.
nodes.evidence_snippet: the EDS elemental mapping images verify that Ru atoms selectively and preferentially anchor on Ni surfaces rather than carbon substrates

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru loading of 2.09 wt% confirmed in NiRu/C SAAs.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometry analysis (ICP-AES) confirmed a Ru loading of 2.09 wt % in NiRu/C SAAs

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD confirms only metal Ni phase in NiRu/C with no other metal phases or Ru aggregation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: XRD patterns in Figure 2a further confirm that, except for metal Ni, no other metal phases are detected in NiRu/C, implying that no Ru species aggregation occurs

nodes.characterization_summary: Single CO adsorption peak at 2084 cm⁻¹ confirms isolated atomic Ru configuration in NiRu; absence of bridge-bonded CO bands excludes clustering.
nodes.evidence_snippet: A single characteristic CO adsorption peak at 2084 cm⁻¹ confirms Ru sites in an isolated atomic configuration, while the absence of bridge-bonded CO bands (2130 - 2140 cm⁻¹) excludes clustering

nodes.characterization_summary: NiRu/C: Ru 3d metallic Ru⁰ at 280.2/284.1 eV and Ruᵟ⁺ at 280.6/284.4 eV; Ni 2p Ni⁰ at 852.9/870.2 eV shifted higher vs Ni/C indicating electron transfer Ni→Ru.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The XPS high-resolution C 1s and Ru 3d spectra (Figures 2c and S16a) revealed two pairs of peaks corresponding to dominant metallic Ru⁰ (280.2 eV for 3d₅/₂ and 284.1 eV for 3d₃/₂) and partially oxidized Ruᵟ⁺ (280.6 eV for 3d₅/₂ and 284.4 eV for 3d₃/₂). The Ni 2p spectra (Figure 2d) indicate metallic Ni⁰ with binding energies at 852.9 and 870.2 eV ... Compared with Ni/C, the Ni⁰ peak in NiRu/C shifts to higher binding energy, demonstrating the electron transfer from Ni to Ru.

nodes.characterization_summary: Normalized Ru K-edge XANES of NiRu/C shows absorption edge position adjacent to metallic Ru foil, confirming predominant metallic state.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The normalized Ru K-edge extended X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra of NiRu/C revealed an absorption edge position adjacent to metallic Ru foil (Figure 2e), confirming the predominant metallic state of Ru.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru K-edge EXAFS shows Ni-Ru coordination shell at 2.1 Å with coordination number 3.69; absence of Ru-Ru (2.4 Å) and Ru-O (1.5 Å) confirms atomic dispersion of Ru.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fourier-transformed extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra indicate that the NiRu/C SAAs exhibit a coordination shell at 2.1 Å attributed to Ni-Ru bonds. The absence of Ru-Ru at ∼2.4 Å and Ru-O at ∼1.5 Å excludes the formation of Ru and RuO₂ clusters/nanoparticles

nodes.characterization_summary: Raman spectra (Figure S7) confirm no perceptible change in surface chemical structure of NiRu-BDC precursor after ion-exchange.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Figure S5), Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectra (Figure S6), and Raman spectra (Figure S7) jointly confirm no perceptible change in surface chemical and crystalline structure after the ion-exchange process.
